articles.title: Couples ‘putting off divorce due to cost of living crisis’ in England and Wales
articles.summary:
Lawyers say financial pressures are fuelling ONS figures that show fewer divorces after longer periods of marriage

Couples are putting off divorce because of the cost of living crisis,…

blocks.text: Couples are putting off divorce because of the cost of living crisis, lawyers have said, after figures showing the average length of a marriage ending in divorce in England and Wales reached a record high last year.

The Office of National Statistics (ONS) released figures on Wednesday showing that the average marriage ending in divorce lasted for 13 years in 2025. This is the longest since records began in 1963 and up from a record low of 8.9 years in 1985.
Rebecca Aston‑Jones, a senior associate at Clarke Willmott, a top law firm that specialises in divorce, said the rising cost of living was keeping unhappy couples together.
“One of the main factors discouraging people from pursuing a divorce is the significant financial pressure that comes with establishing and maintaining two separate households,” she said.

Inflation, which is rising as a result of the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, has pushed up the cost of rent, mortgages and childcare. “It is unsurprising that many people find the prospect of separation financially daunting,” Aston-Jones said.
The ONS figures show there are fewer divorces now than at their peak in the 1980s-2000s, when they reached 150,000 a year.

There were 105,002 divorces in England and Wales in 2025, made up of 102,879 opposite-sex couples and 2,123 same-sex couples. The latter figure was the highest since same-sex marriage was legalised in 2014. There were also 959 civil partnership dissolutions involving 270 opposite-sex couples and 689 same-sex couples.
The head of population life events at the ONS, Greg Ceely, said: “Divorce rates have remained stable over the past few years, but are lower than the peak levels in the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s.
“Our latest findings show that people who divorce or dissolve a partnership are staying in the relationship for longer before it ends.”
Longer marriages were partly because people were waiting longer before they divorce, lawyers suggested.

“As a result, some couples remain in unhappy or hostile living environments, which can be detrimental to everyone involved,” Aston-Jones said. “We are increasingly seeing couples who have separated but continue to live under the same roof so they can retain the benefit of shared assets and continue to split household expenses.

“This arrangement can often exacerbate tensions and create a more volatile home environment. We are also witnessing a growing prevalence of financial abuse within relationships, which can prevent individuals from taking the step to end their marriage because they are concerned about their ability to manage financially on their own.”
after newsletter promotion

Lisa Pepper, a partner and specialist divorce lawyer at Osbornes Law, said: “Divorce is now more accessible than it ever has been in the past 60 years yet these incredible figures show that couples are staying together for a record amount of time.”
She suggested that one “less romantic reason” for marriages lasting longer was likely to be that couples were unable to afford to divorce.

“Couples are more hesitant to get divorced and trying things like mediation or couples therapy before going for the nuclear option as the consequences are often perceived as worse than continuing with their marriage,” she said.
Aston-Jones said there were cheaper ways to get divorced and that seeking advice early could help.

“There are a number of effective alternatives that can help parties reach a resolution outside of court, including mediation and arbitration,” she said. “These methods often provide quicker, more cost-effective, and practical outcomes, enabling families to move forward more amicably, which is particularly beneficial where children are involved.”

articles.title: Taylor Swift announces deluxe version of The Life of a Showgirl with 4 new songs
articles.summary: The pop megastar announced The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore on Wednesday. It's an extended version of her 2025 album and includes four new tracks: Patient Zero, Cleveland!, Pink Clouding and…

image.caption: Taylor Swift attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame induction and awards gala at in New York City on June 11, 2026. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The pop megastar announced The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore on Wednesday. It's an extended version of her 2025 album and includes four new tracks: Patient Zero, Cleveland!, Pink Clouding and Babylon.
Extended album drops on Friday
Put your detective hats away, Swifties. Taylor Swift just looked at her Life of a Showgirl era and said, "Wait, there's more."
On Wednesday, the pop megastar announced The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, an extended version of her 2025 album that includes four new tracks: Patient Zero, Cleveland!, Pink Clouding and Babylon.

"About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave The Life of a Showgirl the biggest first week for an album in history," she wrote on Instagram, alongside brand new cover art featuring the star in a gold fringe minidress on a maroon curtained stage surrounded by glittery showgirl-esque fonts.
The announcement comes shortly after Swift spent the past few days dropping cryptic clues to send her fans into full sleuth mode.

The clues included a countdown on her site and an updated social media bio that read, "And, baby, that's sh0w business f0r y0u. ❤️‍🔥" — the zeros hinting at the title of her next single, Patient Zero.
She also made a cameo in a Law & Order: Special Victims sketch at the 2026 Emmy Awards earlier this month where she offered up a string of words straight to camera for fans to decode and unscramble.

All of it had Swifties spinning over whether she was teasing a deluxe edition, a new project or even the long-awaited Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version) re-record, as her self-titled debut nears its 20th anniversary.

Swift announced the single Patient Zero on Tuesday with yet another Instagram post. Naturally, this prompted another round of fan sleuthing about the scope of the project. Less than a day later, they got their answer.
Swift says the new tracks came together after she went to Sweden to celebrate the success of The Life of a Showgirl with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback.
The duo has worked on some of her biggest hits, including Blank Space, We Are Never Getting Back Together and Wildest Dreams.

items: Taylor Swift's new album is out. What you need to know about The Life of a Showgirl

blocks.text: The celebration apparently turned into another studio session. Because when you're a world-renowned pop star — why stop at 12 songs when you can make 16?
"I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made." Swift wrote on Instagram.
It's official, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce are married
It's been a packed year for Swift.

She married Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce at New York City's Madison Square Garden in July and she's set to take home the first-ever Artist Director award at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards.

A CBS press release says the accolade is "a new award recognizing groundbreaking music artists whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."
The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore is out Friday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
articles.summary: Poland says the aircraft stayed in its skies for 42 seconds, forcing the Nato member to scramble its fighter jets.

blocks.text: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.

Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.

By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.

"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.

Meanwhile in Ukraine, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the border with Poland on 13 September shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

articles.title: Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it
articles.summary: The debate has divided the internet and generations, with some saying that bringing a beverage to a job interview projects an unserious attitude, and others defending their right to remain…

image.caption: A file photo of a Dunkin' Donuts iced coffee in Burbank, Calif. There's a debate raging online over whether or not it's unprofessional to bring one of these to a job interview, and it's dividing generations. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada

The debate has divided the internet and generations, with some saying that bringing a beverage to a job interview projects an unserious attitude, and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.
Some say it projects an unserious attitude. But others defend their right to caffeine
The list of acceptable items to bring to a job interview might include, but isn't limited to: your CV, your portfolio, your winning personality, your best foot forward.

But what about your iced latte? That's the debate currently raging online after a job recruiter recently called out Gen Z for showing up to corporate interviews "with iced coffee, iced latte, in hand" in a now-viral TikTok video.

In the video, which has been viewed more than 420,000 times since it was posted last week, U.S. recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen says she believes showing up with an iced beverage comes across as too casual, "like it's just a stop in your list of errands for the day."
"It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing," Wehniainen said.
"Don't just waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand."
The video has divided generations and the internet, with some agreeing that bringing a beverage to a job interview is unprofessional and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.
"It's not about the f--king coffee,"someone posted on Threads. "It's about reading the room, being able to be part of a community and society, compromise, and tolerate discomfort," they added.
It's about basic etiquette, someone else commented on Reddit.
"Arriving at an interview with a beverage for only yourself would be just as impolite as if the interviewer were drinking coffee but didn’t offer you a beverage," they added.
Conversely, how a company reacts to a beverage is a litmus test, others argued.

"In 2026 being YOU is a competitive advantage, and any environment that tries to micromanage something as small as whether or not you brought coffee to an interview is NOT a place you will thrive," marketing professional Zoë Hartsfield wrote on LinkedIn Tuesday.
"No wonder 58 per cent of Gen Z has a side hustle or runs their own company."
How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak?
Generational divide?

The iced coffee debacle isn't the first time Gen Z has been dragged over etiquette and other so-called soft skills. Last year, the term "Gen Z stare" entered the lexicon, which describes the "blank, expressionless" look that the younger generation gives to older generations, particularly in customer service settings, according to Know Your Meme.

And like the "Gen Z stare," some argue the iced coffee debate touches on deeper issues, like how young adults and teens are coping with the lingering effects of COVID-19 lockdowns while facing the worst youth unemployment rate in decades and having to navigate AI's impact on entry-level jobs and recruitment processes.

items: The 'Gen Z stare' mocks youth for staring into the void, but is anyone laughing?
As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: Gen Z largely came of age during the isolation of the pandemic, tend to prefer digital communication and report higher rates of anxiety than previous generations. Recent surveys have shown that some managers are hesitant to hire younger workers, citing a lack of soft skills like communication and collaboration.
But is the younger generation really bringing iced coffees into job interviews?
Allison Venditti, a Toronto-based human resources expert, says she can count on one hand the number of times it has happened to her, and that's no different to how often it happened 15 years ago.
"We just have TikTok to hear about it now," Venditti, founder of Moms at Work, an advocacy group for working mothers, told CBC News.
"Most folks, Gen Z or otherwise, take the recruitment process seriously and come well prepared and do a great job."
Is the ‘Gen Z stare’ for real?
Is there a middle ground?
That said, Venditti says she does have some iced coffee horror stories, like the time someone brought one in to an interview and accidentally dumped it all over themselves and their papers.
"We spent about 15 to 30 minutes cleaning it up. We also had to find a new room to do interviews as it was sticky. It was awful for all involved," she said.
But maybe there's a middle ground, others argued.

If you do bring an iced beverage into a job interview, don't swirl it around, slurp, put it on the interviewer's desk or hold it in your right hand, since that will make it wet when you shake hands, says Benjamin Chipman, a branding and marketing specialist based in New York City.

"You maybe have one sip that you get to take throughout the entire interview, because that is your opportunity to think a little bit when they are asking you a question," he said in a video posted to LinkedIn.
Which is better than responding with a Gen Z stare, some might argue.
Regardless, the short answer to whether bringing an iced coffee into an interview is unprofessional, is "yes," Venditti says.
"Would you bring a sandwich? No? Then don't bring that, either."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trans row nurse tells tribunal she ‘felt discriminated against’ by her union
articles.summary:
Sandie Peggie accuses RCN of failing to adequately support her in dispute over sharing women’s changing room with trans doctor

A nurse who objected to sharing a changing room with a…

blocks.text: A nurse who objected to sharing a changing room with a transgender doctor has said she felt “discriminated against” by her union after raising the complaint.

Sandie Peggie, who worked for NHS Fife for more than 30 years, won a partial victory against her employer after a tribunal in December 2025, when a judge upheld her harassment claim against the health board but dismissed claims of discrimination, indirect discrimination and victimisation.

Now Peggie has begun a new tribunal proceeding, this time against her trade union, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), which she accuses of failing to adequately support her in her original employment dispute. The union denies all allegations.

Giving evidence on the first day of the tribunal, Peggie said she had originally spoken to her RCN representative, Stuart Fraser, in January 2024 after being placed on special leave by NHS Fife. She told the tribunal: “I felt like he thought I was being disciplined because I had done something wrong.”

Peggie said Fraser was “non-committal” in their first conversation, and did not seem to agree with her that Dr Beth Upton should not be allowed in female changing areas. She said she felt she was being discriminated against and that she was not being supported, but acknowledged she did not say this to Fraser at the time.
She told the tribunal that by February 2024 she had “lost faith” in the RCN, because Fraser had not mentioned legal support in their earlier conversation.

Of the circumstances surrounding her original tribunal claim, Peggie said there had been “general chit chat” among NHS Fife staff about the use of a women’s changing room in Kirkcaldy’s Victoria hospital by Upton.
When asked why no colleagues had given evidence to support her case she said: “I think possibly it was fear … They had seen the way I had been treated at the hospital by senior staff members.”

Peggie’s case further claims that the union refused a request for legal support in January 2025, and that it did not provide adequate support when she asked NHS Fife to commit to ensuring changing facilities should be single-sex.

She argues that the union discriminated against her because of her “gender-critical and sex realist” beliefs. Peggie said: “I felt unsupported. Mainly because I felt I had been discriminated against.”
The nurse has also appealed against the decision from her original tribunal proceedings. That case is expected to be heard in the first half of next year.
The tribunal, taking place in Dundee before judge Melanie Sangster, is expected to continue for seven days.

articles.title: Groceries rise by 7% across Australian supermarket chains, Choice finds
articles.summary:
The price of a basket of items in Coles, Woolworths, IGA and Aldi increased to an average of $43.62, survey says

  • Get our

blocks.text: Groceries have become more expensive at all four of Australia’s major supermarket chains, with the average price of a basket of essentials increasing by 7% between March and June, new analysis has found.

The consumer advocacy group Choice on Thursday released its 10th quarterly government-funded survey of supermarket prices, which it assessed by filling a basket with eight common grocery items at 104 different stores in June.

The basket – containing milk, royal gala apples, strawberries, bananas, potatoes, avocado, basmati rice and beef mince – increased in price by 7% across Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, and IGA since Choice’s last survey in March.
The total cost of the eight items – averaged across all the stores – went up by $2.79 between March and June, from $40.83 to $43.62.

Choice released its latest grocery price survey as the Reserve Bank was widely expected to deliver the fourth interest rate hike of 2026 at its board meeting next week in another attempt to tame inflation.

While the consumer price index – Australia’s official inflation metric – increased by 0.6% in the March-to-June quarter, according to government data cited by Choice, the food categories all rose by more than the overall rate.
Choice found about half of the overall increase came from strawberries, which became 37% more expensive on average over the three-month period – going from $4.68 to $6.41.
There were also higher prices on average for mince, milk and avocados, while apples and basmati rice were cheaper, Choice said.
Overall, the cost of the grocery basket increased the most at IGA, with prices up by 11% on average from $45.42 in March to $50.42 in June.
Aldi had the second-biggest increase at 8% – with the total average cost of the items rising from $37.14 in March to $40.10 in June.
However, Aldi’s basket remained the cheapest overall compared with IGA and the two major supermarkets.

blocks.caption: Choice found about half of the overall price increase came from strawberries. Photograph: Erik Anderson/AAP

blocks.text: At Coles the average total price of the eight items was $42.54 in June, up by 6% or $2.44 since March, when the same basket was $$40.10.
Woolworths recorded the smallest increase in price in the three-month period. At Australia’s largest supermarket chain, the basket went up by 2% or 0.87 cents – from $40.08 to $40.95.
In addition to the base basket of items, Choice also surveyed what it called a “spotlight basket” of 10 items shoppers might buy on a health kick.
In this basket were baby spinach, broccoli, carrots, chicken breast, corn thins, Greek-style yoghurt, hummus, tinned chickpeas and rolled oats.
Choice found that Aldi again provided the best value, with the basket of healthy products costing $28.79.
after newsletter promotion
At Woolworths, the basket cost $33.52, while the Coles basket came in at $34.25. IGA’s basket was the most expensive at $42.27.
In order to work out the average cost for both baskets, Choice mystery shoppers priced groceries at 27 Woolworths, 27 Coles, 23 Aldi and 27 IGA stores.
An Aldi spokesperson said Choice had “once again confirmed that [it] remains Australia’s best value supermarket”.

blocks.caption: Parenting advocate says family pressures are a 'policy failure' – video

blocks.text: “We’re committed to making quality groceries more affordable and helping Australians stretch their budgets further,” they said. In short, we will not be beaten on the cost of the weekly shop.”
A Coles spokesperson said the “vast majority” of its products either remained at the same price or became cheaper between March and June.
“We’ll continue working hard to provide customers with great value, quality and convenience every time they shop with us,” they said.

An IGA spokesperson said it was hard to comment on Choice’s findings in detail without the “full” methodology, but its stores were “more competitive than ever, with many stores matching or beating the major chains on key grocery lines”.
Woolworths was contacted for comment.
The Albanese government has funded Choice to carry out the quarterly surveys of grocery prices since 2024 as one of its cost-of-living measures, with two more reports due under the agreement.
The final two surveys will be the first conducted after the implementation of new laws against “price gouging”, which came into effect on 1 July.

articles.title: West Yorkshire criminals using social media to recruit students
articles.summary:
Organised criminals offer cash to ‘parcel mules’ to transfer illegal drugs, weapons and dirty cash

Students are being recruited by criminals in West Yorkshire to transfer illegal packages…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Students are being recruited by criminals in West Yorkshire to transfer illegal packages containing illegal drugs, prohibited weapons, stolen goods, and dirty cash.

Organised criminals are using social media platforms including Snapchat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit innocent people to help them move illicit goods, particularly targeting students and vulnerable adults.

They are offering cash to “parcel mules” to accept criminal packages in what West Yorkshire police has described as “a new trend,” which could see those not otherwise involved in crime landed with a criminal record.
Parents are being warned to speak to their university age children, and advise them against becoming involved with the gangs moving criminal property around West Yorkshire.
The social media adverts typically contain phrases such as “Work from home”, “Easy money”, “No experience needed”, and “Earn £100-£500 per week”.

Police are warning that the suspect packages could contain anything from illegal drugs to offensive weapons, as well as stolen goods, counterfeit items, or fraudulently purchased products. Some may also contain criminal cash obtained through illegal activities.
Officers have warned that not knowing what was in the parcel may not always protect those handling them from criminal investigation, and ultimately receiving a criminal record.

Depending on what the parcel contains, they may face charges for anything from possession of controlled drugs or prohibited weapons, to handling stolen goods, or money laundering. Anyone receiving the parcels may also find themselves charged with conspiracy offences.

Officers have said that warning signs to look out for include being offered money simply for accepting deliveries, being asked to use your address without being told why, someone using multiple names or addresses, or being asked to accept a parcel but not being told what is inside it.

Police have also said to be wary of anyone saying “don’t worry it’s legal” without further explanation, anyone pressuring the recipient into making a decision, or saying they want to collect the parcels quickly after delivery.

Officers have said that criminals may talk their victims into accepting packages by saying things such as “it’s just because I’m not home during the day,” or “you’re not doing anything wrong,” or “nobody will ever know.”.
West Yorkshire police Chf Insp Michelle Swift said:
“What may seem like an easy favour or a way to get quick cash could leave you facing a police investigation and a criminal record.
“Criminals will often use social media like SnapChat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit people to help them.
“If something doesn’t feel right, trust your instincts and report it to us.
“We hope by raising awareness of this type of crime, people will be alert to the risks and tactics used by organised criminals.
“We would particularly encourage parents to have this conversation with their university age children to make them understand this type of trend and the dangers that are associated with it.”

Earlier this year, Lincolnshire police issued a similar warning, advising people to beware of “anyone offering money or favours for accepting deliveries,” as well as parcels arriving addressed to unfamiliar names, and packages arriving from overseas with no clear sender.
The force warned that in some cases, individuals and addresses are being used without their consent, as part of organised fraud or delivery scams.
Anyone who suspects they may have been recruited as a parcel mule is advised to stop involvement immediately, keep messages, emails or screenshots and report their concerns to the police.
Anyone who has received a parcel not addressed to them is advised not to open it, and to contact the delivery company to arrange return or collection.

articles.title: Property investors may pay less capital gains tax under Labor’s reforms, analysis suggests
articles.summary:
Researcher says public debate since May budget has overstated how much reforms will cost landlords and investors

  • Get our

blocks.text: Most property investors may end up paying less capital gains tax after Labor’s budget reforms, research based on an analysis of historical data suggests.

The e61 Institute’s analysis also found half of all landlords would have faced higher costs from the loss of negative gearing over the period from 2008 to 2025 if the new system had been in place, suggesting the tax reforms alone cannot explain a slump in investment demand.
Under the changes, 53% of housing investors would have paid more tax in total in that period, while 43% would have paid less, according to the research.
Dr Nick Garvin, a co-author of the paper, said public debate since the May budget had overstated how much the reforms would cost landlords.
“The effect on investors is probably not nearly as bad as what’s being made out,” Garvin said.
“If you’ve got 50-50 chance of being better off or worse off, it’s probably not going to affect your decision.”
New investor loan applications fell 28% in two months at the Commonwealth Bank after the budget’s release and July data shows growth in investor credit has slowed.
The Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, said on Tuesday the budget reforms had “very directly” impacted the market.
“[Applications] have really dropped a long way for investors,” Bullock said. “It has changed the dynamic for investors, whether it’s worth them investing in housing or not.”
The e61 research implied the reforms would only slightly add to investment costs, suggesting a much smaller impact on investment decisions than has occurred in reality.
Rising interest rates have also added to costs this year, with another hike expected on Tuesday.
Garvin said some market commentary may have misjudged the impact of the reforms on investor activity because it overestimated investor profits on house sales.

The median home analysed in the paper earned an average annual capital gain of 3.3%, after accounting for sales costs. Garvin’s sample included nearly 921,000 homes, a significant share of all investment properties bought and sold in the period.

Inflation averaged roughly 3% annually from 2008 to 2025, implying a tenth of the median capital gain would be taxable under the new system. Half of the gain would have been taxed under the old system’s flat discount.
“It is possible that a rational investor would see the reforms as beneficial,” Garvin said.

Investors would likely pay more tax under the new system if they borrowed heavily to finance their purchase and invested in properties that rose rapidly in price or had little other income, such as retirees.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, declined to directly comment on the paper but a Treasury spokesperson linked the findings to similar conclusions in the May budget.
“The previous arrangements overcompensated some investors while undercompensating others and we are fixing that with a fairer and more neutral system,” the spokesperson said.
after newsletter promotion
The Liberal shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said the budget’s “cruel twist” was that higher investor costs would be passed on as higher rents.
“Higher taxes will change investor behaviour leading to less housing available for rent and fewer homes being built,” Wilson said.
But Garvin said investors could continue to buy and rent out homes if they prioritised long-term capital gains over short-term cashflow, which had been supported by negative gearing.

About half of all investments are typically negatively geared, running at a rental loss that can be claimed on annual income tax, and most would have paid slightly more tax if the government’s reforms had been in place.

Negative gearing will now only be available for newly built homes, though owners of existing property can still carry forward and claim rental losses on their eventual capital gains tax bill when they sell.
Garvin said part of the post-budget drop reflected that some borrowers had needed negative gearing to afford an investment property.
But the strength of the reaction to the budget suggested investors may not have understood they can still claim losses, leading to “irrational” emphasis on the lost annual tax refund, he said.
Dr Peter Tulip, chief economist at the Centre for Independent Studies, said investors would not be “naive or short-sighted” about negative gearing and come to focus on capital gains.
He said e61’s paper demonstrated that risk-averse investors would find property more attractive, as low gains would now be taxed less and high gains taxed more, making returns more predictable.
“Overall, housing is a safer investment than it used to be,” Tulip said.

articles.title: Gas lobby ‘scare campaign’ urges Victoria to scrap ban in new homes, leaked documents show
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Australian Gas Infrastructure Group lobbying campaign warns energy bills could increase by $100 unless ban is reversed, despite experts disagreeing

  • Get…

blocks.text: The gas industry has been accused of unleashing a “scare campaign” before the Victorian election as it pressures the state government to reverse a ban on gas in new homes.

A paper prepared by a lobbyist for the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) and shared with ministers has warned annual household gas bills could increase by $100 unless the ban is overturned, without providing evidence to support that claim.

From 1 January, all new homes and commercial buildings cannot be connected to the gas network and must instead run on electricity. The government expects this could save households $880 a year – or $1,820 once solar panels are installed.

AGIG – which is owned by a Hong-Kong led consortium – operates and owns major natural gas distribution networks and pipelines in Victoria. The company’s business model will be hit when new homes are not connected to these networks.

The document obtained by Guardian Australia was written by AGIG’s lobbyist, Ken McAlpine, and provides detailed advice on how regulation should be changed, how the ban could be reversed before the election, and how it should be announced to the media.

The document also provides unsolicited political advice claiming a change would neutralise a “key opposition attack line”. The Coalition has pledged to repeal the ban. McAlpine also cites unnamed qualitative research to claim “voters hate the ban”.
The document cites modelling that suggests the government’s ban would lead to a network cost increase of 20% to 40% “primarily due to demand and customer reductions” associated with the ban.
The document claims small businesses and industrial customers could see gas price increases of more than $100 a year.

“AGIG is currently discussing these price increases with customer representatives as part of their regulator price reset process, but these numbers will likely become public by mid-September,” the document says.
The numbers have not yet been made public.
Tony Wood, an energy and climate change senior fellow at the Grattan Institute, said the document was “clearly a scare campaign”.
“I do not understand why there would be any price increases,” Wood said.
In March 2025, AGIG told the state government that network costs would increase for remaining gas customers as more people moved to electric homes.

“We have been warning against that outcome for some time and it should not be allowed,” Wood said. “The consumers who will be ‘forced’ to go electric rather than have a gas connection will be financially better off.”
after newsletter promotion
An AGIG spokesperson said the document was not written by the group but that it reflected its submissions to government and its campaigning on this issue.

Environment Victoria’s chief executive, Jonathan La Nauze, said the letter’s foreshadowing of a price increase – which is set by the independent Australian Energy Regulator and not AGIG – agreed the document was indicative of a “scare campaign”.
“This shows a sophisticated campaign that has considered the political and policy mechanisms,” La Nauze said. “They are very, very focused on getting what they want before caretaker period begins.
“I would absolutely urge and expect Ben Carroll to put the interests of Victorians before the interests of a foreign-owned private gas company.”
When asked about the lobbying document, the Victorian minister for energy and resources, Jaclyn Symes, said the government’s position “has not changed”.
“We’ve always said gas is part of our energy transition – but the reality is legacy supplies from Victoria’s Bass Strait are dwindling and prices are going up,” Symes said.
Francis Vierboom, chief executive officer of the non-profit Rewiring Australia, said AGIG was “trying to do the department’s homework for them”.
“We need to make sure that the government is taking its own advice and following the sensible and nation-leading policies they have already announced,” Vierboom said.

The leader of the Victorian Greens, Ellen Sandell, said “the gas lobby has become so brazen it’s literally written the government a step-by-step playbook for watering down the rules, right down to the media release it wants Labor to send”.

articles.title: Victorian Labor puts reproductive rights on election agenda as it warns One Nation could try to wind back abortion access
articles.summary:
Exclusive: ‘We don’t want to see any winding back of women’s rights,’ health minister says ahead of state election

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Victorian Labor government is announcing new measures to improve access to medical abortion, as it puts reproductive rights on the election agenda and claims One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament.

On Thursday, the deputy premier and minister for women, Gabrielle Williams, and the health minister, Ingrid Stitt, will announce a rollout of new portable ultrasound machines for the state’s 20 sexual and reproductive health hubs.

The machines, costing $480,000, will help confirm early pregnancy sooner, making it easier for women, particularly in regional Victoria, to access medical abortion – a drug-induced termination that can be carried out up to nine weeks’ gestation.

“It means women, particularly in regional Victoria, will be more likely to be scanned within that nine-week window for medical abortion, rather than having to wait or travel long distances to get a scan, and by then potentially only have surgical abortion options available for them,” Stitt said.
Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors.

Stitt said since then Labor had been working to make public abortion care safer – via the introduction of safe access zones around clinics in 2015 – and more accessible, including through the mobile women’s health clinic and virtual women’s health clinic. The latter reported nearly 60% of its appointments in its first year supported medical abortion.

“We don’t want to see any winding back of women’s rights to choose or their access to safe care across the state,” Stitt said. “We’re proud of the investments that we’ve made, and we will be fighting hard to protect them in the election campaign.”
Earlier this month, the Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, emphatically ruled out any changes to the state’s abortion laws under a Coalition government.

It followed the release of a video by a market research company linked to Labor, which claimed that Wilson had “handpicked Liberal candidates who want abortion banned” and stated that One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, wanted to make abortion a crime.

blocks.caption: Warren Pickering. The One Nation Victoria leader said in 2024 that the state’s abortion laws were ‘some of the most draconian on the planet’. Photograph: James Ross/AAP

blocks.text: “Victorians can’t risk a Liberal One Nation government and the polls show the Liberals can’t govern without One Nation,” the video said.
Wilson told the Age: “Abortion law will not change under a Liberal and Nationals government. Full stop.”
She repeated the comments in a video with the Herald Sun at the weekend.
But the deputy premier said Wilson “might not be the one calling the shots”, given current polling suggested the Coalition was short of an outright majority.

“With the way the polling is lining up, this is potentially a situation where One Nation aren’t a minor partner – they’re potentially an equal partner – so her ability to push back on that might be restricted,” Williams said.
One Nation’s national platform pledges to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”.
after newsletter promotion
The federal leader, Pauline Hanson, has said she was not against abortion in the first trimester, a position that has not been reflected in the party’s formal policy.
Last week, its New South Wales leader Mark Newman attended a rally alongside the controversial campaigner Joanna Howe, which was calling for the NSW parliament to restrict abortion access.
At the rally he said One Nation “want to stop” abortion and that if elected, would ensure there was a “right to life … that babies live”.
He later said One Nation does not advocate for an outright ban on abortion and had been speaking about late-term abortions and terminations for sex selection.
Barnaby Joyce appeared at a June event that was organised by Howe, who also campaigned in the lead-up to the Queensland and South Australian state elections.
In 2024, Pickering joined pro-life activists at a “March for Babies” in Melbourne and posted on Facebook that Victoria’s abortion laws were “some of the most draconian on the planet”.

Williams said: “It’s not unreasonable to be asking at what point the Liberal National Coalition are prepared to walk away from One Nation if this is the position they are taking to the election – as their counterparts have in other states.” The deputy premier denied Labor was conducting a scare campaign.
“This is a genuine question being asked on the back of positions that are being expressed by One Nation around the country,” she said. “Where’s the line?”
Pickering has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Iran's president says country won't surrender after Trump threat to 'annihilate' Islamic Republic
articles.summary: Iranian President ‌Masoud Pezeshkian did not mince words in a rare wartime speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he may…

image.caption: Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Sept. 23, 2026. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Iranian President ‌Masoud Pezeshkian did not mince words in a rare wartime speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he may "annihilate" Iran amid the nearly seven-month war on the Islamic Republic.
Iranians have been target of 'cowardly attacks and aggressions,' said Masoud Pezeshkian

In his UN address, Pezeshkian said the Iranian people have been "victims of terrorism" by the United States and Israel, while holding up photos of the more than 150 school children killed on the first days of the war in March, as well as of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian told the annual gathering of ​world ⁠leaders at ⁠the United ⁠Nations.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us."
Pezeshkian said Iran will ‌not surrender in ​the war with ​the United States, ​but believes ⁠in diplomacy ⁠to ‌try to end the ⁠conflict.
"We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he said, adding that Washington does not understand the country it seeks to "bully."
Pezeshkian — who within Iran's political landscape is considered a moderate politician — arrived in New York under heavy security and scrutiny on Tuesday.

items: Trump flexes 'American power' on UN's biggest stage
Saudi Arabia confirms Yemen's Houthi rebels tried to attack its capital with a ballistic missile

blocks.text: Members of the U.S. delegation walked out during Pezeshkian's address on Wednesday. On Tuesday, Iran's delegation had walked out during Trump's address.
On Tuesday, the U.S. president used the same stage to say he faces a "big decision" on Iran.
Trump said one option is making a deal that allows Iran to become a "far greater country" than ever before.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
articles.summary: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

image.caption: The Left Party has always supported the grassroots campaign that led to the 2021 referendum to expropriate property giant Deutsche WohnenImage: Paul Zinken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The socialist Left Party, which won the Berlin election on September 20, was the only major party on the ballot that said it would implement the results of Berlin's 2021 referendum, when 57.6% of Berliners voted to expropriate the apartments owned by real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units.
But the federal government has said they won't let it happen. So is it even possible? And how did we get here? DW explains:

items: What did the Left Party say about expropriation?

blocks.text: The Left Party was one of the main supporters of a successful, years-long grassroots campaign called "Deutsche Wohnen & Co. enteignen," ("Expropriate Deutsche Wohnen").
Deutsche Wohnen is a major property developer that owns over 140,000 units across Germany, and 100,000 in Berlin alone.

The campaign and the Left Party argued that by expropriating this and a handful of other major companies like it, the Berlin government could put some 270,000 apartments in Berlin into public ownership, and make them available at affordable rent prices. Other estimates put the number at around 240,000.
The argument struck a chord, as surveys showed that housing and rent prices were the biggest concerns for Berlin voters in the recent election.
Some 25% of rented property in Berlin is already in public ownership, through state-owned companies like Berlinovo. The expropriation measure would likely push that up to over 30%.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?

items: The 2021 referendum — what was the question and what came out of it?

blocks.text: The original referendum, held in September 2021, asked Berliners to vote yes or no on a five-point plan:
- Socializing the apartments owned by the major property companies
- Administration of the properties by a public-law entity
- Administration of the properties with participation from both city officials, renters, and local communities
- Ban on any re-privatization
- Compensation for the property companies "significantly below" the market value of the property
The referendum did not oblige the state government — at the time a coalition of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party — to immediately implement the plan.

Instead, the then-SPD Mayor Franziska Giffey put together a 13-person expert commission, including former justice ministers and constitutional law experts. This was given the task of establishing whether the plan conformed with the German constitution, or Basic Law, and how the compensation could be organized.
In 2023, the commission concluded that expropriation was legal and possible, though budget questions still needed to be clarified.

By then, a new conservative-led government, headed by the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Kai Wegner, had been voted into office, and announced that it would not expropriate any real estate companies, regardless of what the commission said. At the same time, it emerged that the Berlin CDU was receiving hundreds of thousands of euros in donations from property companies.

Instead, the government said it would draw up a socialization law that would define the conditions for the socialization of property, while ruling out expropriation. A draft law was completed in December 2025.

The Deutsche Wohnen Enteignen campaign rejected this idea as pointless, and had in the meantime gathered legal experts to draw up its own expropriation and socialization law, and promised to start another campaign to force a referendum to implement that.

items: The legal basis for expropriation: Articles 14 and 15 of the German constitution

blocks.text: The original campaign founded its plan on articles 14 and 15 of the German Basic Law.
Article 14 says that, while the right to property is guaranteed, "expropriation shall only be permissible for the public good."

Article 15 states: "Land, natural resources and means of production may, for the purpose of nationalization, be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise by a law that determines the nature and extent of compensation."
As far as the campaigners are concerned, the law they have drawn up covers those two bases.

But, while Article 14 is implemented often enough (for example, when the state wants to build a new highway), Article 15 has never been implemented at all. It is new legal territory, and no one is quite sure what would happen if it were tried.

Some legal experts say the plan would contravene European law. Housing companies would almost certainly fight the measure in court and demand more compensation than the government is willing to offer.
Business Beyond: The global housing crisis

items: 'Not happening' — Chancellor Merz vows to prevent expropriation

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the Left Party's election victory immediately by promising to draw up a federal law banning state governments from expropriating property.

"It's not just about banning something here in Berlin," Merz said at a press conference in the aftermath of the Berlin election. "It's about sending a clear message to international investors, which is: There is no expropriation of private property in Germany."

However, it's unclear whether the federal government has the power to impose such a law. Germany's Constitutional Court once ruled that the federal government cannot pass a law simply to prevent a state from governing in the issues it wants.

items: What now?

blocks.text: The Left Party still has to enter into coalition negotiations to form a government in Berlin. Its most likely coalition partners are the SPD and the Greens, and given the opposition from the federal government and the massive controversy over the issue, the expropriation plan could become a major sticking point.

Whatever happens, the Left Party itself acknowledges that expropriation and socialization would take a while to put into practice, and it would be even longer before it had a measurable effect on Berlin's overall rents.
In the meantime, it has drawn up a number of laws that it hopes will tackle the problem more quickly, such as a rent cap.

In any case, Berliners themselves appear to have gone a little cold on the idea. Despite the Left's electoral success, a recent poll by infratest-dimap found that only 37% of Berliners are still in favor of expropriating real estate companies.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Nike cofounder gives $1bn to University of Oregon in historic donation
articles.summary:
Phil Knight and wife, Penny, make largest known donation to a flagship university to fund a new engineering school

Nike cofounder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the…

blocks.text: Nike cofounder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the University of Oregon in what is believed to be the largest known donation to a flagship university.
The donation, which was first reported by local Oregon media and the New York Times, will go toward the creation of a new engineering school in Eugene.

The University of Oregon’s president, Karl Scholz, said in a statement to local Oregon outlet LookOut Eugene-Springfield on Wednesday morning that the Knights have “a long history of believing in things before they exist” and that “they did it in 2016, and they are doing it again now, at a scale that is genuinely hard to take in. I am grateful to them, and I am grateful to be here for it.”
In the announcement, Knight also shared a statement noting that “to make an audacious dream a reality requires more than a vivid imagination”.
“It also requires the sort of opportunity that our great American universities, both public and private, have historically provided,” he said. “This is no time to abandon them.”
He added: “Penny and I are grateful for the chance to invest in our most promising young people’s future in this important way.”
Knight, 88, is a graduate of the university. The latest donation brings the Knight family’s known total giving to the University of Oregon to more than $2bn, according to the New York Times.

Scholz said in an interview with the New York Times about the donation that “one of the most successful businesspeople in the history of humanity, and one of the most generous philanthropists in the history of humanity, has said higher education is worth an investment of this magnitude.
“At a time when we’re all feeling a little bit under siege, this is tremendous news,” he said, adding that the gift amounted to “a screaming endorsement of the importance of what we’re doing”.
The University of Oregon did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian about the donation.

Bob Guldberg, a vice-president at the university who is also a professor of bioengineering, also told the New York Times that the $1bn donation will allow the university to establish a full undergraduate program that could help address a shortage of engineers in the state.

The news on Wednesday comes as earlier this month it was announced that the Knights were committing $1.1bn to Providence St Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute to create Oregon’s first hospital dedicated exclusively to women’s health.

“Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Knight said in a statement earlier this month. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health. We’re proud to invest in teams that will change what’s possible for communities across Oregon and beyond.”

Last year, Oregon Health & Science University announced that it had received a $2bn commitment from the Knights to its cancer institute, which the university said would “transform the future of cancer care and set a new standard globally”.

articles.title: Ottawa city council votes to dump Trump Avenue
articles.summary: Ottawa city council voted Wednesday to rename a street that was named after U.S. President Donald Trump more than 20 years ago.

image.caption: Trump Avenue is in Ottawa's Central Park neighbourhood where several streets are named after New York City landmarks. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·New
Ottawa city council voted Wednesday to rename a street that was named after U.S. President Donald Trump more than 20 years ago.
City councillor objected to honouring U.S. president in light of Trump's threats to Canada
River ward Coun. Riley Brockington moved to change the name of Trump Avenue at the Sept. 9 city council meeting, saying Trump does not deserve the honour in light of his repeated threats to Canada.
His motion was approved without comment from anyone but Brockington, who said it was time for a new beginning for the street's residents.

Brockington said he will now lead a public consultation process to select a new name for the street in the Central Park neighbourhood off Merivale Road, which includes other New York City-themed names such as Bloomingdale Street and Staten Way.
Brockington said Trump Avenue's new name could stick to that theme.
A working group will be formed to go over options, Brockington said. The goal is to have a new name for the next city council to vote on by April, May or June of next year.

His motion came after Trump imposed tariffs on many billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods and signed an order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America. Canada has retaliated with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports.

A previous effort to rename Trump Avenue in 2021 fell through after a consultation found residents split on the idea, with many who opposed the change expressing concerns about the inconvenience of changing their home address.
With files from Arthur White-Crummey

articles.title: Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
articles.summary: Martin Ryan is pardoned months after he was jailed on charges of spying, but a second Frenchman remains in prison.

blocks.text: French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.

His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.
Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.
However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.
It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.
Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.

Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.

Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".
The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".
Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.

Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".

French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.
Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.
Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.

Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.
"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.
Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

articles.title: White House rolling out red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit
articles.summary: Trump and Xi are expected to discuss a range of issues from trade to AI during the latter's multi-day visit to Washington.

blocks.text: Watch: What’s at stake when Trump and Xi meet in the US?
ByBrandon Drenon
Reporting fromWashington DC
US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with AI, trade and Taiwan expected to be on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers.
Xi will be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on the eve of a White House state dinner and a military flyover.
The three-day trip marks Xi's first state visit to the US since 2015 and his third meeting with Trump in the past year.
Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November.

The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.
Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the forthcoming state visit.
Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances.
He will be accompanied by First Lady Peng Liyuan who is expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with US First Lady Melania Trump on Thursday.
Watch: Rare look at the remote data centres powering China's AI ambitions
David Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented".
"From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China.
"It's quite, quite stunning," he continued.
Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade.
The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data, external.
Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down, external despite the agreement last October.

US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC.
The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking.
US negotiators were expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China's First Lady Peng Liyuan

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
China's First Lady Peng Liyuan

Another likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit.

China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development.
Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late."
Trump's former White House adviser Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI.
The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant.
He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said.
Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration.
On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI.
Several AI and tech industry titans will attend a White House state dinner on Thursday, according to US officials.
Open AI's CEO Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, whose company Nvidia makes chips that power AI, and X boss Elon Musk are some of the dinner attendees.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Open AI CEO Sam Altman at the White House in September 2025

blocks.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Open AI CEO Sam Altman at the White House in September 2025
Experts who spoke to the BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the Trump-Xi meetings this week.
Then there is Taiwan, which remains a diplomatic thorn.
The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China.
Beijing has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force.
Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether.
Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit to discuss deepening US-China trade.
However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter, external to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs.
Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process.
"Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said.
"He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right."
With additional reporting by Daniel Bush, Washington correspondent

articles.title: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc
articles.summary: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it

blocks.text: The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.)

So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”.

Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”.

The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead?

You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has the Ceta free trade agreement with the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump: incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, the renaming of Lake Ontario – all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations.

Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up “laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.)

For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego after Iceland’s recent rejection of more EU accession negotiations.

There’s only one problem: “associate membership” is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”, such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe.

But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days of Jacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration.

Emmanuel Macron’s European Political Community is a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels.

Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an “integrated partnership” – a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+.

Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law, noted that a realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”.

What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty.

Does it, all the same, hold any hope for Brexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display “institutional imagination” at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand.

But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out, the vagueness of the EU offer to Canada might look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK.
after newsletter promotion
A miserable time for Merz

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz needs to rethink policy in order to stay on top. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: Friedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a crushing victory in one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfD made headway in the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. The embattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them.

Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him, a volatile and damaging deadlock will reign in Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear – as a Guardian editorial noted – that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right.
