articles.title: Britain to join the EU’s new global ocean monitoring system
articles.summary:
Cooperation on OceanEye, which will help to predict extreme weather and climate events, comes amid government attempts to move closer to Brussels

Britain is to join a major new ocean science…

blocks.text: Britain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, it will announce today in New York.

The announcement comes as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings that this year’s “supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally.

Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain after threats by the US administration this year to dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations.

In June, the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced an international alliance with Canada as part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations.
In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, will announce the UK is to join the scheme at the headquarters of the United Nations in New York at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister.
Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before.

Eagle will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.”

“Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.”

Joining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements.

The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its $368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiative after a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration.

articles.title: China's 13-year-old swimming star raises questions on child athletes
articles.summary: Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?

image.caption: Yu Zidi has won three golds and set three Games records at the Asian GamesImage: Wu Zhizun/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: The third Asian Games gold medal looked as convincing as the first two, even if Yu Zidi insisted that: "It didn't feel easy at all. It was quite challenging."

On Wednesday, the 13-year-old Chinese swimmer broke the Games record for the third time to add the women's 400 meter individual medley title to her golds in the 200 meter medley and 200 meter butterfly. The three medals add to a bronze she won last year at the World Championships.

Even two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, talk is turning to a potential rivalry with Canada's Summer McIntosh, 20, who herself finished fourth in the 2020 Olympics at 14 and won a world title at 15. As well as their remarkable talent, the pair's youth has raised some questions.
"The first reaction you have when you see something like this is you think, wow, there's a big career ahead," three-time open water swimming world champion Leonie Beck, of Germany, told DW.

blocks.caption: Summer McIntosh is the only person to have swum faster than Yu Zidi in the 400 meters individual medleyImage: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: "But I think maybe this is the problem. People around [the athlete], or maybe the media can create this pressure on a young talent. But just because you're really good and fast at this age, doesn't mean that your whole career will continue like this."
Early success is not always sustained

Beck has already retired from elite competition at 29 and swimming is a sport where athletes often peak early. Katie Ledecky, of the US, and Japan's Kyoko Iwasaki both won Olympic gold at 15 and Japan's Yumeki Kojima, 17, has been a home favorite at the Asian Games, winning a gold and silver in the pool.
While the temptation is to think of Yu as a prodigy, Beck said that to reach the level she has also requires extraordinary dedication and sacrifice.

"My first international competition was in 2011 [at age 14]. At that stage already, I was training eight times a week. You wake up at 5 a.m., by 6 you're in the pool, out at 7:30 so you're in school at 8:00, school until 1, going home, eating, maybe doing some homework, going back in the water training at 3. Then one hour of dry land [training], then in the water again and coming back home at 7 (p.m.). I had this when I was young too."

blocks.caption: Leonie Beck won three world and three European titlesImage: Oliver Weiken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yu, who was discovered by chance by a swimming coach at a water park aged 6, admitted in an interview with state media Xinhua at an event in China in January that the workload takes its toll.
"Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring," she said. "Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating."

While, for Beck, the sporting success made such struggles worthwhile, not all athletes who dedicate their childhoods to their sport reach the pinnacle. The German swimmer added that putting educational, physical and mental support structures in place is critical for sports that allow under-18s to compete.
"Sport psychology should start at a really young age because it should be normal, the same as physiotherapists," she said. "Especially at a young age, where sport should be also fun."

World Aquatics rules state that the minimum age for international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for those fast enough, like Yu. While swimmers peak earlier than athletes in other sports, teenagers at the top level are not so unusual.

In football, Lamine Yamal won the Euros with Spain at 16, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, of India, made his debut in cricket's Indian Premier League at 13 and Nadia Comaneci, of Romania, became the first gymnast to be awarded a perfect 10 in the 1976 Olympics in Montreal aged 14.
Neither are young athletes a modern phenomenon. Dimitrios Loundras remains the youngest ever Olympic medallist, winning a bronze with the Greek gymnastics team in 1896.

While support structures in sport are improving, challenges remain, according to Rosemary Purcell, who played a part in the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) review into youth development ahead of the Paris Olympics in 2024.
"There are pretty stark differences between what we see in the community and in these elite youth athletes," Purcell told DW during those Games.

"Some sports do have a higher rate of eating disorders and body image disturbance in young athletes, but conversely, they may have lower rates of depression and anxiety than we would see in the community."
If you're good enough, you're old enough?
In general, sporting bodies tend to take the approach that if an athlete is good enough, they are old enough. Beck said, allied with the right support, this approach is correct.

"Every athlete has completely different development. Why should you take away the success of a young athlete just because she's young and successful in that age? In my opinion, you should give her the possibility to be successful at that age because maybe, who knows, in a later stage of her career, she will be not that successful. It's not just a solution to say: 'look, you're that age, you're not able to compete.'"

But she also cautioned that because success won't always last, young elite sportspeople should be helped to find a plan away from the pitch, pool or mat, something she struggled somewhat with post Paris 2024.

"You have this idea that, ok, I want to reach the Olympic Games, win this medal. So you have a structure of where to go, what to do. And at one point it's gone and you're like, ‘ok, but now what am I doing with my life? What do I want to reach? What are my goals?'
"It's really, really important that people are starting to think that, 'hey, we are also human beings and you should do something to have a life after the sport because the sport is not endless.'"

articles.title: Former U of Manitoba law dean arrested in France, faces extradition to Canada: police
articles.summary: Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean of the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.

image.caption: Jonathan Black-Branch left his position as the dean of the U of M's faculty of law suddenly in 2020 with no official explanation given. The Law Society of Manitoba disbarred him in 2024. (University of Manitoba)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean of the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.
Jonathan Black-Branch facing Canada-wide arrest warrant for fraud
Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean at the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada.
Winnipeg police spokesperson Const. Stephen Spencer confirmed Wednesday the arrest happened in France and the matter is currently before the French court system.

Police can't say more while the matter is before the courts, he said in an email, but "further information will be provided should the extradition application be successful" and Black-Branch is returned to Winnipeg.
He could not confirm when Black-Branch was arrested.
Black-Branch, who was hired as U of M's law dean in 2016, left his post suddenly in 2020 with no formal explanation given.
Around the same time, an internal investigation by the university, based on a whistleblower complaint, found a senior university employee misspent university funds.

items: Former U of Manitoba law dean disbarred in U.K., still under Canada-wide arrest warrant

blocks.text: In 2023, a months-long law hearing by the Law Society of Manitoba found Black-Branch had committed professional misconduct and misspent more than $600,000.

He spent U of M endowment funds on expensive meals at the members-only Manitoba Club, personal education at Ivy League schools, accommodation, travel and other expenses while he was dean of the U of M's law school, according to the society's decision.
The U of M then asked Winnipeg police to investigate for possible criminal charges.
The law society disbarred Black-Branch in 2024, removed his name from its rolls of barristers and solicitors, and fined him $36,000.

While overseas in August 2020, the University of Southampton, in the U.K., announced Black-Branch as the new head of its law school. Days later, the university changed course and announced it would no longer be hiring him.
Earlier this year, Black-Branch was disbarred for a second time.

The Bar Standards Board for England and Wales barred him from practising law, citing his actions in Manitoba as "blatant and sustained dishonesty," according to the disciplinary decision by the Bar Tribunals and Adjudication Service.
The Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued for Black-Branch on March 30, 2026, on a charge of fraud over $5,000.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: New York and Boston face weekend nor’easter with high winds
articles.summary:
First such storm of fall could have wind gusts of 70mph in places, flooding and power outages, forecasters warn

New York, Boston, and much of New England could face a weekend nor’easter…

blocks.text: New York, Boston, and much of New England could face a weekend nor’easter storm with wind gusts of 70mph in places, and “significant” impacts including beach erosion, flooding, and power outages, forecasters warn.

Effects from the season’s first such storm since Tuesday’s official start of fall could last through the weekend, especially if the system sits swirling off the coast, a scenario experts say is looking increasingly likely.

“If the storm nearly stalls, several days of persistent onshore winds and pounding surf could take a significant toll on beaches and vulnerable coastal communities, especially with astronomical high tides coinciding,” said Alyssa Glenney, an AccuWeather meteorologist.

The online weather service predicted “a long-duration storm for many areas along the mid-Atlantic and New England coasts”, with impacts beginning late Wednesday, spreading to New England late Friday or Saturday, and lasting through Sunday in some places.

The Weather Channel said coastal flood alerts were in place across the mid-Atlantic, and winds were likely to bring sea rise up to 3ft above normal levels. But it said uncertainty remained about exactly where the system would be at the end of the week.
“Forecast models are picking up on the low, but two models show that the timing and duration of the storm could differ,” the Weather Channel said on its website, weather.com.

“The European model brings the low close to the coast as a strong storm, but it moves slower. It could even meander around the east coast until it fizzles. Under this scenario, there would be more time for strong winds to cause significant power outages, heavy rain-induced flooding, and coastal erosion.”
The GFS model, meanwhile, brings the storm in faster, and approaching New England by Saturday afternoon.

“A faster storm could mean winds, rain and coastal erosion would be less severe and lessen disruptions to travel and weekend plans,” the Weather Channel said. “However, this model calls for a stronger storm by the end of the weekend as it moves away from the north east, meaning some coastal areas could experience longer-lasting impacts.”

Nor’easters are more prevalent from September to April, the National Weather Service said. They usually develop within about 100 miles of the cost between Georgia and New Jersey, and progress steadily north eastward, typically attaining maximum intensity near New England and the maritime provinces of Canada.
AccuWeather’s forecasters agreed with the Weather Channel that the exact track of this weekend’s storm remained important for communities farther inland.

“A track closer to the coast could bring heavier rain, stronger wind gusts and travel disruptions from Washington DC and Philadelphia, to New York City and Boston, while a track farther offshore would limit inland rain and wind impacts,” the service said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 29: Court overturns initial 16-conviction threshold in VP trial
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually…

blocks.text: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.
On July 6, presiding officer Senator-judge Francis "Chiz" Escudero set the number of votes needed to convict at 16, or two-thirds of all the 24 senators.
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution does not state a number and instead reads, "No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”
The same constitutional provision also states that "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment."
Those who voted in favor of Tulfo’s motion are:

items: Paolo Benigno "Bam" Aquino IV
JV Ejercito
Sherwin Gatchalian
Risa Hontiveros
Panfilo Lacson
Lito Lapid
Francis Pangilinan
Vicente "Tito" Sotto III
Erwin Tulfo
Raffy Tulfo
Joel Villanueva
Mark Villar
Juan Miguel Zubiri

blocks.text: Of the 13, only Senator Villar is from the Minority bloc.
The lone no vote came from Escudero.
The six minority bloc senators who did not participate in the vote are:

items: Alan Peter Cayetano
Pia Cayetano
Christopher Go
Imee Marcos
Robin Padilla
Camille Villar

blocks.text: Defense team lead counsel Sheila Sison said the Vice President’s camp will exhaust all legal remedies to address the new threshold for conviction, among other things.

"She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available sa ilalim ng ating batas at Konstitusyon na may pagtatangi sa esensya ng isang tunay na malayang, demokratikong institusyon. At karapatan ng bawat mamamayan na madinig sa isang hukuman na walang kinikilingan o kinakatakutan," she added.

(She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available under our law and Constitution, with due regard for the essence of a truly free, democratic institution. And it is the right of every citizen to be heard in an impartial court that fears no one.)
Alan Cayetano attempted to defer the voting, to no avail.
No acquittal by default

Ahead of the vote, House prosecutor Chel Diokno of Akbayan party-list said the threshold must be changed since the Vice President’s case should be decided on merits, not by default or absence of senator-judges.

“Yes, the Constitution deliberately makes conviction harder by imposing the two-thirds requirement. But making it harder is not the same as making it depend on senators who are not judges or who are incapable of acting as judges. That would be tantamount to an acquittal by default, a failure to arrive at the threshold number caused not by the judgment of the incapacitated senators, but by their mere inclusion in the denominator,” Diokno added.
Defense counsel Michael Poa, however, said that the July 6 ruling of Escudero setting 16 votes as the threshold cannot be appealed since it is not provided under Senate impeachment rules.

“Last July 6, 2026, on the very first day of trial, the presiding officer ruled that a voting threshold to convict is 16. At that time, no senator-judge objected. No senator-judge sought reconsideration. No senator-judge appealed. Your Honors, that was over two months ago. There is no supervening event. Our point is, nothing changed between July 6 and today,” Poa said.

Escudero, however, had a rebuttal for Poa by citing the Supreme Court decision in People v. Amigo, GR number 116719, which states that Supreme Court decisions are “not petrified rules grown rigid once pronounced, but may be reconsidered upon further reflection in light of new perspectives.”

“The July ruling issued during an ongoing proceeding is not a final judgment on any Article of Impeachment. It cannot claim greater; therefore, this issue cannot claim greater immutability than the judicial doctrine itself. Where the governing impeachment rules prescribe no period and no final judgment has been rendered, the court remains free to reconsider its interpretation,” Escudero said.

Erwin Tulfo also addressed Poa’s comments that there is no supervening event, citing that their four colleagues being detained due to alleged plunder, being in hiding from authorities and being on leave are something that the court should address as elected representatives of the people.
Camille Villar then appealed to his colleagues not to attack their detained fellow senators, saying that they are not yet convicted of their alleged crimes.
Her take was seconded by his brother, Mark Villar, citing that there should be respect among colleagues.
Erwin Tulfo apologized if his comments offended his colleagues, but he stressed that he never said their colleagues were convicted of crimes.
“What I said was they were charged in court,” Tulfo said.

“Further, the statements were not attacks against our fellow senators but merely confronting the present reality that some senators are physically or legally unable to participate in the impeachment trial. The issue of detained senators is so intertwined in the determination of the denominator,” Tulfo added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Young Australians are staying in the family home for longer – and it’s not hard to see why
articles.summary:
Housing costs are up with renters worst affected and financial stress is also growing, according to the largest survey of its type

  • Get our

blocks.text: Every year, thousands of Australians answer a series of questions as part of the long-running Hilda survey.
This questionnaire – more expansively known as the household, income and labour dynamics in Australia survey – has been tracking the same households since 2001.

As the families have expanded over the past two decades, the survey has grown to include about 17,000 people a year in 9,000 households, offering a unique insight into Australian life in the 21st century – and how it has changed.
This week, the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, which manages the survey, published its annual snapshot of the social and economic trends shaping Australia.
Here are six things we learned.
Half of young Australians are living with their parents
The trend is clear: leaving the nest has become ever harder.
In 2001, 39% of people aged 18-29 were living at home with their folks. Fast forward to 2024, and that figure is just shy of 50%.
Young men are more likely to live at home than women, but that gap has shrunk a bit over the 23 years. And 36% of 18- to 29-year-olds living at home in 2024 are full-time students.
It’s also notable that the big shift towards staying at home happened through the first decade of the century.
More of us studying for longer is one answer, but so is the mounting cost of moving out, which we’ll turn to a bit further below.
One group is being left behind
Employment rates reached record highs in 2024, with the survey showing 84.4% of working-age men and 76% of working-age women had jobs.
Aussie workers are better educated – more than half of women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree.
Men are better educated now than at the start of the century, too, but in every age group women were found to be “considerably better educated than men,” the report said.
But there is one group where employment outcomes have become much worse.
As Kyle Peyton, a co-author of the report, says: “Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force”.
“Their full-time employment rate fell from 70% in 2001 to 63% in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12% to 22%,” Peyton says.
Women who never finished high school – and did not achieve any other higher education – have also dropped out of the workforce at greater rates: from 40% in 2001, to 48% in 2024.
That’s not as sharp an increase, but still much higher than for men.
Household income has trended higher this decade …
The pandemic, the huge lockdown payments from governments, and the post-Covid inflationary outbreak has made for a bumpy ride.

Median disposable (or after tax) household incomes peaked in 2021, before being pummelled by soaring living costs from 2022. The Hilda survey shows the typical household was earning less in 2024 than the recent peak in 2021, but more than in 2019.
Looking longer term, the survey shows household incomes lifted strongly through the first decade of the century, before plateauing right up to the pandemic.
… but financial wellbeing is down
Australians report lower financial wellbeing on average than they did before Covid-19, despite higher median household incomes.
As Inga Lass, the lead author of the report, says “the post-pandemic shock to cost-of-living is clear”.
There were declines in reported financial wellbeing across age groups between 2020 and 2024 – except for the over-65s.

The survey asked five questions and asked people how well it described them from one (“not at all”) to five (“completely”). The researchers then converted this to a wellbeing score out of 100 (where the higher the number, the higher the wellbeing).

The share of people who could enjoy life “not at all” or “very little” due to their money management lifted from 11.3% in 2020 to 12.7% in 2024. And in 2020, 62.1% agreed or strongly agreed that they felt on top of everyday finances; by 2024 it was 58.5%.
And while 60% of people in 2020 agreed or strongly agreed they were comfortable with their current spending relative to the money coming in, that share had dropped to 53.8% in 2024.

“These results imply that worsening perceptions of meeting shorter-term ‘every day’ financial outcomes explain a sizeable shift in the reported decline in financial wellbeing over the four-year period,” the report said.
Housing costs are higher …
Of course, we all know that the cost of keeping a roof over your head (and your family’s) has been a major factor in the new era of high living costs.
The Hilda survey shows weekly mortgage payments – including principal and interest – jumped between 2021 and 2024 to reach new highs as the Reserve Bank jacked up interest rates.
Fast forward to today, and the RBA has reversed the three rate cuts it made in 2025, which means the burden on mortgage holders is similar to when the last survey took place.
The survey shows weekly private rental costs were pretty steady through the 2010s, but have since climbed higher and higher.
And while overall household incomes are lower than they were in 2021, housing costs are higher – which has heaped pressure on many Australians.
Housing stress is particularly acute for renters in the regions
The Hilda survey uses the “30-40 rule” to measure housing stress.
A household is in housing stress if housing costs are more than 30% of disposable household income, and the household is in the bottom 40% of households by disposable income.
Among the cities, renters in Sydney are the most likely to be experiencing housing stress, with more than 31% meeting the definition in 2024 – that’s about twice the rate in Adelaide.
The next toughest market is in Brisbane, with 26% of renters in housing stress. Across the mainland capital cities, one in four are in housing stress.
As high as those rates are, the share of regional renters in housing stress is substantially higher at 30%, and nearly double what it was before the pandemic.
In contrast, about one in 10 mortgaged owners are in housing stress, and that number has generally held steady over the past 20-plus years.

items: Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

articles.title: DoJ backs Trump ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now, citing security concerns
articles.summary: The news organizations, which sued the US president, are claiming the ban violates the first amendment

blocks.text: The US Department of Justicehas defended Donald Trump’s decision to ban three new organizations from the White House in a court filing, arguing that access to the grounds was a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.

Lawyers for the US president doubled down on Trump’s claims about CNN, Politico and MS Now reporting “Fake News” and insisted the ban did not violate the first amendment because “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right”.

In the court filing, justice department lawyers argued that Trump had concluded the news outlets “fail to satisfy the minimum requirements of professionalism” by relying on anonymous sources, and not giving the White House enough time to comment.
Trump’s lawyers also claimed the three organizations had violated “decorum” by publishing classified or sensitive national security information.
The justice department asked Timothy Kelly, the federal judge overseeing the case, to allow Trump to enforce his White House ban on reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now.
The judge is expected to hold a hearing on the new organizations’ request for a temporary restraining order on Wednesday at 3.30 pm ET.

CNN, Politico and MS Now sued Trump on Monday, days after the president announced he would institute a White House ban on all three for reporting “fake news” – an accusation the US president has repeatedly made against media outlets, often without citing evidence.
The three news organizations are asking judge Kelly to stop Trump from enforcing his ban and to restore their hard passes to the White House, claiming the ban violates the first amendment.
But Trump and his justice department insist the ban does not infringe on the right to the free press; rather, it addresses “national security” threats.

In Tuesday’s filing, lawyers for the justice department said it sent letters to CNN, Politico and MS Now on 22 September outlining examples of reports that violated “the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex”.
The letters cited various “reporting incidents”, including some that “threatened national security and spread falsehoods”.

That includes CNN’s reporting on construction of the East Wing bunker under the White House ballroom; MS Now’s reporting on an alleged leak investigation; and Politico’s reporting on how the US Secret Service would invest money into security improvements for Trump’s ballroom.

articles.title: Pakistan's jailed former PM Khan's sons told DW the authorities are cracking down ahead of new PTI protests
articles.summary: The sons of jailed Pakistani ex-PM Imran Khan told DW their father is in ill-health while being isolated from family and doctors. Other family members have been detained ahead of a planned opposition…

image.caption: Despite being jailed since 2022, Khan remains a popular political figure in PakistanImage: K.M. Chaudhry/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Family members of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan are concerned about the 73-year-old's health in a Rawalpindi prison, accusing authorities of preventing him from accessing appropriate medical care.
Khan's London-based sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, told DW they have received "little to no information" about their father's health condition.
"When we last spoke to him on the phone back in March, he said that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye and that despite his complaints, it was neglected for months," they said.

The brothers added that their father was being held in a tiny cell and has been allowed outside for only one or two hours a day. They also allege that the elder Khan was kept in isolation from family, lawyers, and a personal physician for 10 months before he was briefly allowed to see two of his sisters.
This comes amid the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's planned protest march on September 27 to exert pressure on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government for Khan's release.
Sons demand family access and medical care for Khan
Khan's sons are urging authorities to allow their father to receive an independent medical assessment and restore regular access to his family and medical team.

"We are asking the Pakistani authorities to obey the Supreme Court orders immediately and shift our father to Shifa International Hospital so that he can be assessed by independent doctors," they said.
They also called for Khan to be allowed his mandated family visits, phone calls with his sons, and access to a personal physician.

blocks.caption: Pro-Khan protesters clashed with authorities during a 2024 protestImage: ASIF HASSAN/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Khan's sisters detained as PTI plans new protests

Despite being in jail, Khan remains at the center of Pakistan's political confrontation between the PTI and the country's powerful military. He also remains a popular political figure in Pakistan, despite being ousted from office in 2022 in a parliamentary no-confidence vote.
Amid plans for a PTI protest march set for this weekend, Khan's three sisters were detained in the Punjab capital of Lahore on Monday.
The detention orders cited concerns that the sisters were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public order. All three were ordered to be held for 30 days under a public order ordinance.
Khan's sons told DW the arrests were intended to intimidate their family and supporters before the planned protest rally.

"Our family members who have been arbitrarily taken into custody must be released immediately," they said. "The abductions of our family members in the middle of the night, with no reason given, were purely to intimidate them," they added.

Khan was ousted as prime minister in 2022 and jailed the following year on what he says are politically motivated corruption charges. Khan's family members, and his PTI opposition party, have faced an ongoing government crackdown.

blocks.caption: The detention orders for Khan's sisters cited concerns that they were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public orderImage: AAMIR QURESHI/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan government calls for 'order'
Pakistan's government has rejected the PTI's characterization of the crackdown and says its priority is to maintain public order during the planned protest.
Talal Chaudhary, Pakistan's minister of state for interior, has warned that the government will not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"If you are a peaceful citizen, come to Islamabad from any route, come 100 times," Chaudhary told DW.
"But if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave," he added.

In 2024, pro-Khan protests on the streets of Islamabad turned violent. Demonstrators breached high security zones and clashes with security forces, leaving six dead. When Khan was first arrested in May 2023, nationwide PTI support rallies also led to violence, with military and government buildings suffering damage. Several people were killed and hundreds injured.
Chaudhary said the government would not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"The right to protest does not give the right to attack," he said.

Authorities have stepped up security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi ahead of the protest, including the deployment of thousands of police personnel and the placement of shipping containers and other barriers at key entry points.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Arrests could 'galvanize' PTI supporters
The PTI has said the September 27 protest will demand Khan's release and push for what the opposition describes as respect for constitutional and political rights.

Michael Kugelman, a South Asia analyst at the Washington-based Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, told DW the arrests will likely further energize Khan's supporters ahead of the planned protest.
"The arrests will galvanize what is already an angry and anxious Khan support base," Kugelman said.

The detention of Khan's sisters, who Kugelman said are "prominent advocates" of Khan's cause, has also placed his family increasingly at the center of the confrontation between the government and the PTI.
Khan's base is "concerned about the state of his health, and for his sister to be detained will increase the chance that protesters take to the streets on the 27th," he added.
Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader and close aide to Khan, said the arrests were meant to create fear but will not prevent the party from mobilizing its supporters across the country.
"What they don't realize is all they are doing is creating more hatred for themselves among the public," Bukhari told DW, referring to the government.
Bukhari described the current crackdown as the most severe the PTI has faced. "This crackdown seems the more brutal," he said, adding that the government was acting out of frustration.

"They are fueling a fire that will soon be out of their control," asserted Bukhari. "They can keep attacking us, and we will continue to resist. This protest will go on, and many more after it," he added.

As Pakistan's government is dealing with several challenges, including economic malaise, conflict with the Afghan Taliban, and fallout from the Iran war, further domestic unrest would be an unwelcome complication.
Pakistan: 'Security state' on the rise amid regional tension

Eala is expected to draw a huge crowd in her round of 16 clash against Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova at Centre Court of the OCBC Arena on Thursday, September 24, after her packed fan event.
Throngs of fans, including Singaporean locals, flocked to The Kallang on Wednesday, September 23, to catch a glimpse of Eala during her Q&A session — a testament to her growing star power.

blocks.text: Sitting at a career-high No. 18 ranking, Eala earned a first-round bye as the third seed and will battle Prozorova coming off a much-needed break following her run to the third round in the US Open.

articles.title: Slovakia: PM Robert Fico's NATO Article 5 remarks spark criticism and raise questions about his country's NATO commitment
articles.summary: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico says he fears war and will do everything he can to keep his country out of one. Critics say his remarks risk weakening NATO, the alliance that was designed to…

image.caption: 'I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,' said Slovak PM Robert FicoImage: Martin Baumann/TASR/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I'm afraid of war," Robert Fico told medical students at a teaching hospital in Presov last week.

"What is happening in Europe today, what we're hearing and seeing today, is that the military conflict in Ukraine has got out of control," he went on, warning them that Europe faced the possibility of a wider war.

He asked the students to imagine Slovakia being told to prepare "5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers" who would go somewhere to fight "without us even knowing whom they are fighting, or why, or what for."
Then he turned to Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
"I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5," Fico said.

"Yes, we are in NATO. We value that. Cooperation and fulfilling our obligations matter to us. But as prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."

blocks.caption: Czech President Petr Pavel has questioned whether Fico understands the meaning of the word 'solidarity'Image: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: The remarks prompted uproar from the Slovak opposition and also a spat with Petr Pavel, president of neighboring Czechia and former chairman of NATO's Military Committee.
"If anyone says they're glad to be a member of NATO … but are unwilling to get involved if anyone else is attacked, then they have not understood the word solidarity," Pavel said.
Fico replied that he understood that Pavel, as a former NATO general, would like to fight, while he himself preferred peace.
The impact on Slovakia's standing
The Slovak prime minister's fear of a wider war is shared by many Europeans. But critics at home gave his remarks short shrift.

"Isn't he a prime minister? Isn't he the leader of a country? Is he not supposed to lead people instead of expressing fears?" asked former Slovak Foreign Minister Miro Wlachovsky, now a distinguished fellow at the GLOBSEC think tank.

blocks.caption: Slovak PM Robert Fico (left) and Czech PM Andrej Babis (right) have both stressed their preference for diplomacy when it comes to ending the war in Ukraine Image: Jaroslav Ozana/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: "My question for him as prime minister is: OK, even if the situation is as bad as you are saying, what I want to hear from you is how the country is prepared. What have you done for preparedness? Who will come to our aid in case we are attacked?" Wlachovsky told DW.
Asked whether Fico's remarks could damage Slovakia's standing among its allies, Wlachovsky replied: "It's already done."
Political background to Fico's comments
Analysts see a clear political context to Fico's remarks.

The Slovak prime minister will face a difficult reelection fight next year. Some observers believe Fico is trying to steal votes from the extreme-right Republika party, which is viscerally hostile to NATO and the EU and opposes military support for Ukraine.

Wlachovsky compared Fico's rhetoric to that of Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban and the current Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, both of whom have presented themselves as the candidates of peace.

Babis was heavily criticized during his unsuccessful 2023 presidential campaign after questioning during a televised debate whether the Czech Republic should send troops to NATO ally Poland if it came under attack.
What is NATO's Article 5?
Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former NATO spokesperson, told DW that Article 5 was "the most solemn pledge that a country can make to another."
But its central purpose, she said, was deterrence: convincing a potential aggressor that it would face the alliance together, rather than an isolated member.
"This is about solidarity, standing together, underpinning deterrence and therefore avoiding war," she said. "NATO is a defensive alliance. It's not an offensive alliance."
Nor would invoking Article 5 automatically send every member's troops into combat, she said.

The North Atlantic Council, where every ally is represented, would assess an attack and decide by consensus whether it constituted an Article 5 situation — Slovakia's voice would be equal to that of its 31 partners in that room, she said.
Once consensus was reached, each country would then assist the attacked ally by taking the action it deemed necessary, which might — or might not — involve armed force.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, following the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
Lungescu pointed to one of NATO's initial responses: sending AWACS surveillance aircraft to patrol US skies and help prevent another attack.

blocks.caption: Solidarity: Slovakia's neighbors and NATO allies Poland and Czechia in 2022 pledged to protect Slovak airspace.Image: Petr David Josek/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: She pointed out that Slovakia already benefits from the same solidarity Fico appeared to question. The country hosts a NATO multinational battlegroup established after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with personnel from several allies alongside Slovak troops.
Its purpose is to deter an attack on Slovakia.
'Exactly what Putin wants'
For former Slovak Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad, the danger lies in allowing that fear to dictate policy towards Ukraine.
"This is exactly what Vladimir Putin wants," said Nad, who was defense minister from 2020 to 2023 and is now head of the non-parliamentary opposition Democrats party.

"He wants citizens in the EU and NATO to believe that if EU and NATO countries continue to support Ukraine, this escalatory situation might lead to a Third World War or something like that," Nad told DW.

Nad was in office when Slovakia decided to hand over its entire fleet of ageing MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine. Fico's government later sought a criminal investigation into the transfer; prosecutors closed the case, finding no crime.

"Even when I was defense minister, I heard this not only from ordinary people but also from some ministers around the table: that we shouldn't help Ukraine with this or that equipment or capability or ammunition, because it might create a difficult situation in terms of escalation towards Russia," he went on.
"None of that happened."
Could Slovakia replace Hungary as EU's main disruptor?

articles.title: Germany's oldest party, the center-left SPD, is in a difficult position following its success in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has vowed to press ahead with controversial reforms, but resistance is mounting within his coalition partner, the SPD. How much dissent can a governing coalition…

image.caption: Manuela Schwesig is the new center of power in the SPDImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, two of Germany's 16 federal states, the mood within the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) is oscillating between relief and frustration, confidence and bewilderment. "The SPD is clearly capable of winning more than 30% of the vote," party co-leader Lars Klingbeil said jubilantly in Berlin. "This result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is an encouragement for the entire Social Democratic movement."

As Klingbeil put it, Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and her party had shown "how to make up ground, how to fight, and how, with the right issues and the right approach, to stage a comeback and ultimately win people over through that effort."

What Klingbeil conveniently omits is that Schwesig's success was also due to the fact that she distanced herself as much as possible from the federal government's policies, and by extension from the SPD at the national level, which it governs in coalition with the center-right CDU/CSU alliance of the Christian Democratic Union and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union under Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The national government has meanwhile become more unpopular than any of its predecessors.
Me or the AfD: SPD state premier presents a stark choice
Focus on the SPD's traditional values

Schwesig scored points above all with her opposition to parts of the federal government's pension reform plans. At the post-election review meeting in Berlin, she intensified her criticism, launching a pointed attack on the chancellor. She argued that 81% of people in her state consider the reforms unfair and that Merz is misjudging the situation.

On election night, Friedrich Merz made clear that he was all the more determined to stay the course. "The reforms must go ahead," the chancellor said. "Of course, this puts all of us in a difficult position. What needs to be done now requires courage, resilience, and patience. I will demonstrate those qualities as leader of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."

Schwesig had a clear response. "My advice to the chancellor, if he wants to regain people's trust, though I'm not sure that's still possible, is that he needs to engage with the reality on the ground." She argued that Merz must ask himself what needs to change. "There can be no business as usual."
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
Bas and Klingbeil struggle to chart a course

The SPD, and above all its leaders, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas, now find themselves in a dilemma. Both serve as cabinet ministers in Merz's government and therefore help implement policies that many SPD members are increasingly questioning.

At the same time, they are accountable to their party and must ensure that SPD priorities are reflected in government policy. The success Schwesig achieved with her unequivocally critical stance is now putting them under considerable pressure.
Following her electoral victory, Schwesig has emerged as one of the most influential figures within the SPD. Many party members would like to see Schwesig become the party's next leader.

She already seemed to be stepping into that role as she stood before the microphone at the post-election review, dressed entirely in red and projecting confidence. By contrast, Bas and Klingbeil appeared almost defensive, seeking to strike a balance between criticizing the coalition and supporting it.

"If people in our country perceive reforms as something that threatens their way of life and leads only to things getting worse, then it is not just our communication that needs to improve. In some areas, the substance of the reforms themselves needs to change as well," said Klingbeil.
Bas called for both a "reality check" and a "fairness check" on the reforms, arguing that they must be workable in practice and socially equitable.
Show confidence, uphold socialdemocratic values

Will that be enough? Calls for the SPD to be "more like Schwesig", in other words, to assert its own positions with greater confidence, are growing ever louder within the party. The only question is how much dissent a governing party can afford to show. "Nothing would be more damaging than allowing this coalition to collapse over a policy dispute at this point," Bas warned. Solutions, she argued, "are possible within this coalition as well."

At a leadership committee meeting on the morning after the state elections, the SPD leadership adopted a strategy paper. Across nine key points, it sets out the priorities the party intends to champion in government. One section is headed "Real Change Instead of Simply Cutting Spending", while another is titled "An Affordable Life for All".

The SPD wants inheritance tax reform to ensure that the resulting revenue can fund a "genuine education initiative". On pension reform, the paper states that important questions remain unresolved regarding phased retirement and the right to retire without pension reductions after 45 years of contributions.
The SPD therefore makes its position clear: "The lifetime achievements of people who have paid into the system for many years must continue to make a difference."

It remains unclear whether the CDU/CSU will respond to these demands. The same is true of the simmering debate over whether Bas and Klingbeil should be replaced at the helm of the party. Pressure continues to come from Philipp Türmer, leader of Jusos, the SPD's youth wing. "I'm not saying that the two of them are the problem, but at the moment they're not part of the solution either," he told German broadcaster RTL and its news channel ntv.

Türmer and others had called for a special party conference that could have paved the way for replacing Bas and Klingbeil. Instead, the party will hold only a convention in December, a smaller party gathering that cannot elect or remove party leaders. From now on, however, SPD members are likely to judge their leaders even more by how effectively they defend the SPD's positions in government and whether they can restore the party's appeal among voters.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Discord, Reddit given more time to establish Philippine offices, says CICC
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday said that it gave Reddit and Discord more time to put up their respective offices in the Philippines after the platforms…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 9:12pm

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday said that it gave Reddit and Discord more time to put up their respective offices in the Philippines after the platforms expressed their willingness to work with the government in addressing online threats.

The CICC on Tuesday gave both platforms 24 hours to establish a Philippine presence within 24 hours to enhance collaboration with the government following the shooting at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato.
Reddit said that it would establish an office in the Philippines, while Discord reached out to say that it was willing to work with the CICC to address the issue.

“We decided to grant them an extension since they responded within the 24 hours, and we want to give them the opportunity to work with us because what we want is accountability and a clear mechanism for government to coordinate with the platforms,” CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato “Aboy” Paraiso said in a statement.

“While we welcome their commitment to work with us, we will not settle for anything less. This commitment must translate into concrete action, genuine accountability, faster response mechanisms and stronger protections for our Filipino children online,” he added.

The online meeting was attended by Reddit Vice President of Policy Jessica Ashooh, Deputy General Counsel Leslie Liu and Policy and Regulatory Affairs Manager Vijay Pamarathi. They discussed establishing “green lanes” or direct lines with Philippine authorities wherein the latter could flag potentially harmful content.
This would also involve online sexual abuse and exploitation of children (OSAEC), child abuse and exploitation materials (CSAEM), and Nihilistic Violent Extremism (NVE).
Discord told the CICC that the newly rolled out Global Teen Experience would ensure that teenagers are placed in age-appropriate places on their platform.

Discord Senior Public Policy Advisor Vasundhara Singh said that users who cannot be placed in a specific age group will have to confirm their age through facial age estimation, with biometric data not being stored in Discord.

The shooting in South Cotabato is the third school shooting incident in 2026. In June, two students opened fire in a high school in Tacloban, killing three others. Not more than two months later, in August, another student shot and killed a schoolmate in Ateneo de Zamboanga before turning the gun on himself. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Canada’s Mexico visa requirements limit country’s tourism potential, says tour operator
articles.summary: The Canadian government sees Mexico as a growing market for tourism and projects visits to rise by 40 per cent over the next four years, hitting nearly half a million visitors spending about $1…

image.caption: Jesus Martinez, left, general manager of Dream Destinations Mexico, meets with Tobias Barth, who co-owns Whitehorse’s Northern Lights Resort and Spa, during a business-to-business 'speed-dating' event in Mexico City on Sept. 22, 2026. (Tania Miranda Perez/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

The Canadian government sees Mexico as a growing market for tourism and projects visits to rise by 40 per cent over the next four years, hitting nearly half a million visitors spending about $1 billion a year by 2030.
Federal agency hosted business-to-business encounters between tour operators in Mexico City
The visa requirements Canada has imposed on Mexicans limit the full market potential the country offers as a source of tourists, according to a Mexican tour operator.

While the number of Mexicans visiting Canada is growing, the visa requirements reimposed in the late winter of 2024 had an immediate impact on the figures, said Jesus Martinez, general manager of Dream Destinations Mexico.
"We haven’t recovered the numbers that we would love, but the numbers are going up," said Martinez in an interview with CBC News.
He said scrapping the visa is on his "wish list," but he isn’t holding his breath waiting for the change.
"It’s not up to us," said Sanchez, whose company builds tour packages it sells to agencies and individuals.
The government under prime minister Justin Trudeau initially lifted the visa requirement for Mexicans travelling to Canada in 2016. His government then reimposed the requirement, under U.S. pressure.
Mexicans are eligible to enter Canada by air under an Electronic Travel Authorization if they hold a valid, non-immigrant U.S. visa or have held a Canadian visa in the past 10 years.
'Untapped' potential

Martinez was attending a type of speed-dating event this week for Canadian and Mexican tour operators at a Mexico City hotel hosted by Destination Canada, the federal Crown corporation responsible for promoting Canadian tourism.
Canadian and Mexican tour operators participated in 12-minute rounds of one-on-one meetings to build ties and business opportunities.

items: U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator
Alberta beef entering Mexico’s Costco market where U.S. cuts once reigned

blocks.text: During one of the rounds, Martinez sat down with Tobias Barth, who co-owns Whitehorse’s Northern Lights Resort and Spa.
"If we think about the aurora [borealis] viewing, how does that work on a day-to-day visit?" said Sanchez.

"That’s a really good question," said Barth. "The big benefit of being at Northern Lights Resort and Spa in the Yukon is that you don’t have to go anywhere … [Tourists] can see the northern lights right out of bed."
Barth told CBC News that Mexico is currently the resort’s fourth-largest source country for customers, behind U.S., domestic and Australian visitors.
Darlene Fedoroshyn, executive director of international marketing with Travel Alberta, said Mexico is a potential source of one million visitors a year for the province.
"The potential is pretty untapped at the moment," said Fedoroshyn. "The numbers are staggering, and so what we have to do is try to convert that."
Fedoroshyn acknowledged that the visa requirement could be a stumbling block for some Mexicans seeking to visit Canada.

"We always want to advocate for making it easier to come into Canada and we would work really hard with our federal government and with our [provincial] government to try to make it simpler for travellers," she said.
Mexican visitors at pre-pandemic levels

Canadian federal Tourism Minister Rechie Valdez attended the Destination Canada event. Valdez, who is also minister of women and gender equality, was scheduled to meet with Mexico’s secretary of tourism on Wednesday.
Valdez sidestepped CBC's questions on whether Canada would consider rescinding the visa requirement for Mexican visitors.

She said Canada is now seeing pre-pandemic levels of Mexican tourists and that the numbers continue to grow. Valdez said she would share any feedback she receives during her time in Mexico with her cabinet colleagues when she returns to Ottawa.
"It’s really important for us to ensure that we are doing everything we can to promote the growth and strength of our tourism sector," she said.

articles.title: This N.L. town's single electric bus has been out of service for almost a month, and people are fed up
articles.summary: The town's transit service, which launched in June 2025, operates through a single, 18-seat electric bus that has been out of service since Aug. 27.

image.caption: Happy Valley-Goose Bay's electric bus, the sole bus in the town's transportation network, has been out of service since Aug. 27. (Town of Happy Valley-Goose Bay)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
The town's transit service, which launched in June 2025, operates through a single, 18-seat electric bus that has been out of service since Aug. 27.
Town's electric bus has been out of service since Aug. 27
It's been nearly a month since Happy Valley-Goose Bay's single electric bus went out of service, and two residents say their frustration only continues to grow.

Stephanie White rode the bus almost every day to work at the Valley Veterinary Clinic. But since the bus went out of commission on Aug. 27, she said she's had to give up shifts in recent weeks because she lacks another mode of transportation.
"It's frustrating, because I need to get to work. And now I'm paying $20 for a cab each way to my other job," White told Labrador Morning.
"I've talked to a few people, and they said that it's a great service when it works. But it's not working enough for it to be worth the amount of money that the town sunk into it."
The town's transit service, which launched in June 2025, operates through a single, 18-seat electric bus that runs between Happy Valley and Goose Bay.
In an interview with CBC News on Tuesday, Happy Valley-Goose Bay Mayor Bert Pomeroy said the town is waiting for parts from overseas to fix a mechanical issue.
"We're kind of at the mercy of the shipping company, so we're just waiting on that. I haven't received an update today, but as far as I know they're in transit," he said.
"Hopefully those parts will arrive soon, and we'll get our bus back on the road."
The service outage has also caused problems for students like Rihanna Stone, who recently moved to the community and was hoping to rely on the bus for transit without a car.

items: Mark your calendars: The HVGB town bus has a launch date

blocks.text: "It's very hard to get to one point or another, especially if 'Oh, your hospital's on one side or your pharmacy is on one side, and you live on the other side.' It's a minimum of, like, a 15-minute drive. So it's hard for me, and any other people who are also facing this issue, to get anywhere," Stone said.
"If you don't have a car, and you're moving to Goose Bay without knowing what it's like … then it becomes an issue."
People shouldn't be dependent on one-bus service: Mayor
Both Stone and White said they'd like to see secondary transit options in the community, or something that better fits the infrastructure of Happy Valley-Goose Bay like a gas or diesel bus.

Pomeroy said that's likely out of the question, as operating one bus is already costly. He said it has cost around $230,000 for the year, and that a secondary bus — especially one that operates on diesel — would be even more costly to taxpayers.
With the town operating just one bus, Pomeroy said he believes the town's transit system is more of a supplementary tool — and that residents shouldn't rely on it as a main mode of transportation.

"I don't think people should be dependent on this service. You know, we have one bus, and we have a large community. You know, the bus is available on-demand, when it's available. You know, we can't make a bus appear when somebody wants one," he said.

"We're very proud of the service we provide. Is it 100 per cent service? Can't guarantee that. We can't guarantee the bus won't break down next month. So, you know, that's the realities that we're in."

articles.title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez hails ‘historic meeting’ with Donald Trump in New York
articles.summary:
Interim president, who agreed a 65bn-barrel oil deal with the US, did not say whether she would visit her snatched predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, in jail

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy…

blocks.text: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.

The former foes met at a five-star hotel in Manhattan a few blocks from Trump Tower late on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas.
On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.

But Venezuela’s interim leader did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.

“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally.

Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which both he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.
A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as she appeared to wince.

Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appears to be clenching her left fist as she poses beside the grinning US president.
Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against Yankee imperialism.

After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of major concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.
One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez/Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.

blocks.caption: Observers suggested Delcy Rodríguez’s clenched left hand signified her discomfort around Donald Trump. Photograph: Venezuelan Presidency/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.

Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week, but failed.

Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.

At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.

As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.

Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.

“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for fresh elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

articles.title: Questions swirl as members of Belleville, Ont., synagogue return after shooting
articles.summary: Some members of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., took their first steps into the building Tuesday since the fatal shootout nearby on Sunday night.

image.caption: Norm Weddum, president of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., points at bullet holes in a synagogue window on Sept. 22, 2026 (Michael Cole/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa
Some members of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., took their first steps into the building Tuesday since the fatal shootout nearby on Sunday night.
Its president says they want to celebrate officer injured by the gunman
"It's kind of eerie to first step back in here," said Norm Weddum, president of the synagogue.
"We're all kind of looking at the damage … it's kind of surreal."
Congregants gathered at the synagogue for Sunday's Yom Kippur services were forced to take cover on the floor around 7 p.m when a gunman fired at a police officer in an unmarked car outside.
Const. Jeff Smith suffered serious injuries during the shootout with the 29-year-old shooter, Sean Ward, and a second officer who joined the exchange, officials said in a Monday news conference.
Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said Tuesday Smith remains in stable condition and that Ward died Monday night.

items: Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says

blocks.text: Weddum said he counted two dozen bullet holes in the synagogue's street-facing stained-glass windows.
He added that while he is glad to be allowed back in, he fears Ward's death will leave the community looking for answers.
"I'm kind of sad he died because I really wanted to find out his motive.… The police would have eventually questioned him."
The investigation into Sunday's events is ongoing. It's unclear if the shooting was targeting Smith, Sons of Jacob or the city's Jewish community.

A spokesperson for the Department of National Defence said Tuesday that Ward joined the Canadian Armed Forces in July 2017, that he served as an infantry soldier with Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry and was a corporal when he was released in June 2022 without having been deployed.
Neighbours near Ward's home in neighbouring Quinte West said he mostly kept to himself.
Sheri Skanes said she sometimes saw him playing with a dog in the backyard.
"I just think it's horrendous," she said of the shooting. "It's really sad what's happened."
Kevin Burley said he didn't know the suspect personally, but did have two "confrontations" with him about speeding where he said Ward responded in a way that was "very aggressive."
Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting near synagogue dies in hospital
Seeing police cars parked in their neighbourhood and hearing about the gunfire has been "very difficult to deal with," said Burley.
"Thank God the police officer was there to save these people. In my opinion, he is a hero. I hope he has a speedy recovery."
Weddum said one of the first things members of the synagogue want to do is celebrate Smith once he's recovered.
The congregation of roughly 35 families is focusing on moving forward, with many feeling relief they can soon get back into the building and run programs and services, Weddum said.
Members still have to decide when to fully reopen and there are plans to eventually do a larger community gathering.

She holds a master's degree in international journalism from City University of London, and also studied journalism, law and political science at Carleton University. articles.title: Zelenskyy to address UN, Rubio to meet Russian counterpart — but few breakthroughs expected
articles.summary: Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations, just hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addresses the United…

image.caption: Firefighters extinguish a fire at a burning building following a Russian drone strike in Kyiv on Wednesday. (Danylo Antoniuk/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations, just hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Kremlin rejects idea of summit with Trump, Putin, Zelenskyy

At least two people were killed and 22 were injured ​in the morning attack, according to city authorities, in one ​of the heaviest strikes since Russia began attacking Kyiv and nearby areas over the summer with faster and high-flying jet drones that are harder to intercept.

Zelenskyy met with U.S. President Donald Trump Tuesday on the UN sidelines, where they discussed a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets and asked for increased supplies of U.S. Patriot air defence missiles to defend against an expected Russian winter campaign against Ukraine's electricity infrastructure. No agreements were reached, he said.

Trump said last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to strike energy targets, but any semblance of a truce disappeared when petrol stations in Kyiv were struck the following day and Ukraine bombed a Russian oil refinery.

For his part, Zelenskyy has said ‌he was ready for "any format" of an energy ceasefire with Moscow, as long as Russia halted its own attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure — something he doubts the Kremlin will honour.
Trump urges pause on energy attacks after Ukraine, Russia trade strikes

The Kremlin cautioned on Wednesday ahead of a planned meeting in New York between U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov that there were still no grounds for Ukraine peace talks to take place.
"For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

items: Trump and Zelenskyy discuss potential for energy truce in face of new wave of strikes on infrastructure

blocks.text: Peskov said Russian President Vladimir Putin stood ready to meet Trump one-on-one if both leaders deemed such a meeting necessary. But he made it clear that Russia's stance on the possibility of Putin and Zelenskyy meeting in person had not changed.

The Kremlin has said that Zelenskyy would need to come to Moscow for such a meeting having already taken decisions Russia has been pushing for — an idea that Kyiv has repeatedly dismissed as unacceptable, suggesting any talks could only be held in a neutral country.
Peskov also played down the idea of a trilateral summit with the three presidents.
"Generally speaking, in any other circumstances, it would be inappropriate to hold a summit meeting before the groundwork has been laid at expert level, as this would be a waste of time," he said.
LISTEN | Victor Jack, NATO reporter for Politico, on latest tensions:
Front Burner26:05Why Russia has Europe on edge
U.S. ponders diesel export ban
France's President Emmanuel Macron said Monday he had discussed with Trump initiatives aimed at securing a moratorium on attacks linked to the energy sector.

The French leader said helping Ukraine's energy system remained a priority as the war continued to affect security across Europe and he hoped progress could be made during the annual gathering of leaders at the United Nations.
While Trump has blamed the attacks for soaring diesel prices in the U.S., most economic experts believe the U.S.-initiated Iran war has been a bigger factor.

items: Ontario farmers raise issue of high diesel prices with politicians at plowing match
Sky-high crude and diesel prices are fuelling protests worldwide

blocks.text: Trump said Tuesday he backed the idea of a diesel export ban supported by some Republican legislators in agricultural states. But it's not unanimously supported by all Republican members of Congress and it puts the president at odds with his own energy officials, who warn it could raise fuel prices on the coasts and tighten supplies for European allies.
"If you start putting barriers ​on flows, pretty quickly you will reduce the production, and you'll have less supply. We need more supply, not less supply," U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said that a ban would be unlikely to lower petroleum prices and ⁠could lead to retaliatory measures by energy exporting countries, which states like California rely on for some of their energy.
In a Tuesday interview with Fox News, Rubio suggested there was another reason for the U.S. concern about the strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

"The one thing we are concerned about, however, is that over the last few months, on a number of occasions, American-linked ships, American oil supplies have been targeted, probably not deliberately, but targeted nonetheless by Ukraine," said Rubio, not specifying which U.S. companies he was referring to.

items: Putin's ruling party romps to win in wartime Russian election

blocks.text: In Russia, the Economy Ministry expects the country to produce and export less natural gas this year than previously forecast, according to a draft government document seen by Reuters. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Russia had also downgraded its 2026 oil output forecast to a 17-year low and revised the fuel export outlook for this year and next due to the war with Ukraine.

Natural gas production and export forecasts have been revised down against the background of ruptured economic and political ties with the West over the Ukraine war and the European Union's plans to stop all purchases of Russian gas from next year. Russia's gas exports to Europe tumbled 44 per cent last year to the lowest amount since the mid-1970s, according to Reuters calculations, following the closure of the Ukrainian transit route.
